extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, screenwriters, filmmakers, and students of story craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative standards for designing, writing, and revising screen stories—focusing on substance, structure, style, audience, originality, and craft. Applicable to writers creating or assessing screenplays and dramatic stories for film and related media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is about principles, not rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule says, 'You must do it this way.' A principle says, 'This works ... and has through all remembered time.' The writer must master principles rather than blindly obey rules or imitate formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles are stable guiding tenets that allow many valid expressions; rules are rigid and limiting. Avoid anxious obedience to rules or rebellious breaking of them—master the form so you can adapt principles to each work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is about eternal, universal forms, not formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single prototype or paradigm that guarantees commercial success; great films show astounding variety yet share an underlying universal form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on 'foolproof paradigms' or recipe books. Study the deep, changeless form of story across cultures and genres instead of following trending formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetype over stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal story unearths a universally human experience wrapped in unique, culture-specific expression; stereotypical story confines itself to narrow, cliché-ridden generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek archetypal conflicts (e.g., dependence vs. independence) rendered in fresh, specific detail so the story 'travels' across cultures. Anti-pattern: substituting well-worn settings, characters, and actions that limit audience empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness, not shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: From inspiration to last draft may require as much time as a novel; writing economically (brevity) takes time and perseverance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite ruthlessly to express the absolute maximum in the fewest words. Beware of assuming a screenplay is quicker or easier because of its short page count; brevity is achieved through sustained effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft is knowable; embrace realities not mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Storycraft is not arcane; principles have been public since Aristotle. The screen offers no hiding place—camera x-rays falsity—so the craft must be learned and applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study technique and practice scene-by-scene rigorously. Accept that problems can be solved through study and application rather than mystification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the art rather than second-guessing the marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: You can't reliably predict what will sell; instead, write with surpassing quality. Excellence attracts agents and producers; polished work reduces tampering in production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on making your script director- and actor-ready via patient rewriting. Anti-pattern: trying to write to formulas believed to 'sell' or panicking about market trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the audience; design for sophisticated anticipations
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect audience intelligence—audiences are often 'smarter than most films' and anticipate events. Shape story to both express your vision and satisfy audience desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep ahead of the audience's sharp perceptions; avoid underestimating viewers. Failure to account for audience reaction undermines story effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality is content plus form; avoid mere duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality arises from distinctive subject matter combined with unique arrangement/telling. Eccentricity for its own sake is not originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align fresh substantive choices (setting, character, idea) with innovative formal choices (structure, progression, point-of-view). Anti-patterns: novelty as a gimmick, or slavish replication of past hits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenwriters must express the maximum with the fewest possible words; economy is a sign of craft and takes time to achieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut repeatedly; prefer concise description and dialogue. Example: Pascal's comment — short, powerful writing requires more effort than long-winded prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing story is the primary labor (who, want, obstacle, consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 75% or more of a writer's effort goes into designing story: who are the characters, what do they want, why, how they pursue it, what stops them, and what are the consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat story design as an analytic and imaginative craft—answer the grand questions and shape them into progression. Anti-pattern: lavishing time on dialogue/description while neglecting these core design questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression, motivation, and protagonist clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A story must progress (cause-effect), have believable motivation, a discernible protagonist, and integrated tensions/subplots that contribute insight and character revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid convenient coincidence, weak motivation, unrelated tensions, flat characters, and lack of insight. McKee's 'PASS ON IT' checklist: first 30 pages avoiding fat exposition; main plot must be driven, motivations must be strong, characters must be revealed to be more than they seem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spectacle over substance
rubrics_metrics.description: When storytelling declines, creators substitute spectacle, trickery, or sensationalism for truthful, principled story—yielding hollow pseudo-stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize honest satire/tragedy and meaningful drama over excessive imagery, gratuitous violence, or noisy sound design that mask weak story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn craft through study and apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: Novices too often rush to write without studying theory and practice; historically writers learned via libraries, theatre experience, studio apprenticeship, or university instruction in intrinsic dramaturgy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue deliberate study of story principles (dramaturgy), read classical texts, seek mentorship/apprenticeship, and develop intrinsic methods rather than relying solely on 'instinct' formed by passive exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values and moral clarity anchor story
rubrics_metrics.description: Values—the writer's perception of what’s worth living or dying for—are at the soul of a story. In an age of cynicism and relativism, the writer must dig deeply to uncover convictions to express to a skeptical audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to articulate meaningful value judgments through story design; avoid assuming shared values—build them into the work through character, conflict, and consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content must mutually inform each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Content (setting, characters, ideas) and form (selection and arrangement of events) require and inspire one another; shaping one will reshape the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterate between substance and structure—rework substance to support design and play with shape to evolve the story's intellectual and emotional spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't confuse eccentricity with originality (avoid gimmicks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference for difference's sake is empty; avant-garde quirks or infantile gimmicks that call attention to the artist undermine the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mature artist avoids flashy devices used merely to show off. Ensure formal or stylistic choices serve the story's deep meaning rather than self-display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial form reveals personal cosmology
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyteller's selection and arrangement of events functions as a 'master metaphor' revealing his insight into life's interconnectedness; form can identify an artist as surely as content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal choices (protagonist count, rhythm, levels of conflict, temporal arrangement) intentionally to embody your vision. Study masters whose forms consistently express personal worldview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting and polish preserve integrity in production
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure writers rewrite until scripts are mature; polished, mature work resists tampering in production while unfinished work invites interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect producers to fix foundational story weaknesses. Avoid selling first drafts; invest in multiple rewrites to make the script actor- and director-ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is the dominant measure of a screenplay
rubrics_metrics.description: The Story Department's focus is story quality—not merely dialogue, description, or formatting; a good story makes a good film possible while poor story guarantees disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or submitting material, prioritize story problems (lack of progression, false motivation, redundant characters, empty subtext, holes). Good dialogue and images won’t save a weak story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience as co-determinant of design
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience's reactions and anticipations are as determining of story design as any element; shaping story must consider audience desires without pandering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance personal vision with an understanding of how audiences will engage emotionally and intellectually. Use audience sensitivity to calibrate revelation, pacing, and surprise.
